claims.text: The starting mixture contains Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, and Ti in equiatomic proportions.
The proposed process uses approximately 6 hours of high-energy ball milling followed by SPS at 1000°C for 10 minutes under 50 MPa.
Approximately 6 hours of high-energy ball milling produces nanoscale grain refinement.
Approximately 6 hours of high-energy ball milling produces severe lattice strain.
Milling-induced lattice strain and grain refinement lower the activation or thermodynamic energy barrier for the FCC/BCC transition.
SPS at 1000°C facilitates densification of the milled powder.
At 1000°C, configurational entropy thermodynamically stabilizes the FCC phase.
The proposed milling and SPS conditions suppress Ti-rich HCP precipitation.
VEC and atomic-radius mismatch jointly govern the FCC/BCC phase stability window in CoCrFeNiTi.
The fine grain size inherited from milling inhibits grain growth during SPS.
Sluggish diffusion in the multicomponent alloy suppresses the segregation and diffusion needed for phase decomposition or precipitate growth.
Milling-induced grain refinement increases hardness through the Hall–Petch effect.
The resulting CoCrFeNiTi compact will be fully dense.
The resulting microstructure will be single-phase FCC or FCC-dominant.
The processed alloy will have significantly higher Vickers hardness than cast CoCrFeNiTi.
Cast CoCrFeNiTi typically has a mixed FCC/BCC/HCP microstructure.
Grain growth becomes dominant above a system-specific SPS threshold likely near 1100°C.
Exceeding the proposed temperature boundary increases the volume fraction of Ti-rich HCP phases.
In another mechanically alloyed HEA system, milling beyond 20 hours did not cause further powder phase changes even though grain refinement continued.
Vickers testing at a low load such as 0.1 kgf isolates grain-boundary strengthening from precipitation hardening.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says increasing temperature makes entropy-stabilized FCC dominant over enthalpy-driven HCP formation, whereas the boundary says that increasing temperature beyond roughly 1100°C allows the thermodynamic driving force for Ti-rich HCP formation to overcome FCC entropy stabilization. This reversal in temperature dependence is not reconciled.
